nodes.name: Car dynamics update
nodes.purpose: The per-tick vehicle update: wheel contact rays, suspension travel, driveline and tyre impulses, driver aids, aerodynamics and the rollover recovery path, all applied to a single rigid body with four ray-sprung wheels

nodes.name: Tyre force model
nodes.purpose: Slip ratio and slip angle from wheel and contact velocities, then longitudinal, lateral and self-aligning forces from a magic-formula curve family, including camber shift, combined-slip scaling and a precomputed table of peak-force slip values

nodes.name: Suspension and wheel kinematics
nodes.purpose: Coilover springs and dampers, travel limits and overtravel, steering axis with caster and Ackermann, toe and camber offsets, and the sampled hinge kinematics for double-wishbone, strut and simple trailing-arm layouts

nodes.name: Engine, clutch, gearbox and differential
nodes.purpose: Engine torque from an interpolated curve with friction and rev limiting, clutch torque capacity, gear ratios and shift timing, and the limited-slip differential ratios that feed the wheel shafts

nodes.name: Wheel contact constraints
nodes.purpose: One three-row impulse constraint per wheel: a softened spring row for suspension travel, a rolling row along the wheel heading and a lateral row, limited by the tyre force budget and by the wheel shaft inertia; also the surface description those rows read

nodes.name: Rigid-body world and surface ray casting
nodes.purpose: The fixed-step rigid-body world the cars live in: substep budgeting, gravity, downward wheel ray queries that resolve a hit point, normal, penetration depth and a pointer to the track surface

nodes.name: Track strips, patches and surface queries
nodes.purpose: Bezier road patches joined into strips with a bounding-volume index, ray intersection against a patch subdivided into a parameter quad tree, strip closure detection and sector bookkeeping

nodes.name: Opponent drivers
nodes.purpose: Per-tick opponent logic: read the patch under the car, derive a corner speed limit from curvature and friction, run a braking lookahead along the strip, steer toward a lookahead point and rate-limit the resulting throttle and brake

nodes.name: Generated racing line
nodes.purpose: An offline pass over the road strip that nudges a lateral lane value at every sample until the curvature is minimised, producing the reference path and the per-sample curvature used by the drivers and the drawn racing line

nodes.name: Lap and sector timing
nodes.purpose: Per-car lap and sector clocks, staging countdown, best-lap records keyed by car type, drift score accumulation and the running placement ordering used for the results screen

nodes.name: Fixed-step game loop
nodes.purpose: The fixed logic tick that drives AI, car input, the physics world, car state consumers, track objects, timing, particles and force feedback in a fixed order, with a wall-clock catch-up budget

nodes.name: Camera rigs
nodes.purpose: Chase and orbit camera behaviours: an offset frame carried by the car orientation, a blend toward the target position, a look-at orientation, and an orbit rig with clamped yaw, pitch and distance

nodes.name: Driver input mapping
nodes.purpose: Binding-aware analogue shaping applied before the car sees any input: dead zone, gain, response exponent, invert flag, and a signed ramp that turns a button press into a gradual analogue axis

nodes.name: Car and skid-mark visuals
nodes.purpose: Interpolated body and wheel transforms taken from the physics read-back, steering and brake-light state, and the skid-mark emitters whose energy accumulates from tyre squeal intensity

nodes.name: Replay recording and playback
nodes.purpose: An input-delta stream plus periodic car state snapshots, replayed by feeding recorded inputs back into the same car dynamics so playback stays consistent with the live run

cards.name: Fixed logic tick and substep budget
cards.summary: A 90 Hz logic tick, a ten-substep rigid-body budget and ten internal driveline substeps with four solver passes
cards.behavior: Game logic advances in fixed steps rather than by variable frame time. The loop accumulates wall-clock time and runs one logic step per ninetieth of a second of simulated time, capping the number of catch-up steps it will attempt so that a slow frame degrades the frame rate instead of the simulation. Inside the physics world the step is handed to a solver that may split it into up to ten substeps, and inside the car each tyre-and-driveline pass is itself resolved in ten substeps with four impulse iterations per substep. The practical consequence for feel is that wheel spin, clutch lock and tyre force limits stay stable at speed, and a car that is pushed into a wall never explodes, because the cheapest resolution is always a fraction of the fixed tick.

constants.name: logicTickRate
constants.unit: logic steps per second (one step each 1/90 s of simulated time)

constants.name: minimumFrameRate
constants.unit: frames per second before simulated time is discarded, evaluated once per 1/90 s tick

constants.name: maxRigidBodySubsteps
constants.unit: substeps per 1/90 s logic tick

constants.name: drivelineSubsteps
constants.unit: substeps per 1/90 s logic tick, giving a 1/900 s internal step

constants.name: solverIterations
constants.unit: impulse iterations per substep, resolved every 1/900 s

constants.name: gravity
constants.unit: metres per second squared used in grip and braking arithmetic, read once per 1/90 s tick

cards.name: Downward wheel rays and suspension travel
cards.summary: Four downward rays find the ground; penetration depth past the wheel radius becomes the suspension displacement for that tick
cards.behavior: Every tick four rays are cast downward from points offset along the body, each starting above the wheel hub by one wheel radius, and each is given four metres of reach. A hit supplies a contact point, a surface normal, a penetration depth and a pointer to the surface. The suspension is then driven by a displacement computed from the geometry rather than from the ray distance directly: twice the wheel radius minus the reported depth, so a wheel whose hub sits exactly one radius above the ground rests at zero travel and a wheel pressed into the ground gets positive travel. Any surface bump is added at half amplitude. This makes the whole car body a single rigid mass riding on four ray springs, so ground clearance, wheelbase and ride height come out of the ray geometry rather than from a special-case vehicle solver.

constants.name: contactRayLength
constants.unit: metres of downward reach per ray, cast once per 1/90 s logic tick

constants.name: radiusToDisplacementFactor
constants.unit: wheel radii, giving travel = 2 x radius - penetration depth, once per 1/90 s tick

constants.name: surfaceBumpShare
constants.unit: fraction of the surface bump amplitude added to travel, once per 1/90 s tick

cards.name: Airborne wheels and rollover recovery
cards.summary: A wheel with no ground hit contributes no force, and a car tilted past roughly forty-five degrees can be righted and dropped back onto the road
cards.behavior: When a wheel ray finds nothing, the contact is still constructed but flagged as a non-contact with no surface and no hit, so that corner contributes no suspension force and no friction for that tick: the car is genuinely airborne from that wheel outward, and a jump therefore behaves like a thrown rigid body rather than a magnetised car. If the whole car leaves the road, all four corners fall into the same state and only gravity and aerodynamics act. Recovery is a separate explicit path. A reset places the car along the down axis until the lowest wheel is exactly one radius above the ground and zeroes both linear and angular velocity, which is what makes a respawn land cleanly. A rollover request compares the car up axis with the world up axis and only rotates the car when the tilt is at least forty-five degrees, so a car leaning on a kerb is not silently flipped back upright.

constants.name: worldGravity
constants.unit: metres per second squared on the world up axis, integrated every 1/900 s substep

constants.name: rolloverRecoveryThreshold
constants.unit: divisor of pi radians giving the tilt threshold (pi/4, about 45 degrees), checked per reset request

constants.name: resetGroundClearanceFactor
constants.unit: wheel radii used when measuring the lowest wheel, evaluated per reset request

cards.name: Anti-roll bar coupling
cards.summary: Opposite wheels on an axle share a spring rate proportional to their travel difference, with a stiffness floor and a hard bump-stop term past full travel
cards.behavior: Wheels are handled in axle pairs. For each pair the model takes the difference between the two displacements and converts it into an added spring rate on the compressed side and a negative one on the extended side, scaled so that a car rolling into a corner stiffens the loaded corner and softens the unloaded one. The combined spring plus anti-roll rate is floored just above zero, so the extra term can never invert the spring and start pulling the body down. When a wheel runs past its published travel the excess is treated as overtravel: it is added to the displacement and a very stiff bump-stop term is folded into the spring rate, which produces a sharp, non-linear stop instead of the wheel sinking through the body.

constants.name: wheelsPerAxlePair
constants.unit: wheels sharing one anti-roll rate, recomputed once per 1/90 s tick

constants.name: antiRollRateDefault
constants.unit: newtons per metre of left-right travel difference, once per 1/90 s tick

cards.name: Steering lock, Ackermann and assist
cards.summary: Steering is a normalised command scaled by per-wheel lock, bent by an Ackermann term and optionally clamped to the tyre peak slip angle at speed
cards.behavior: Driver steering arrives as a single value between full left and full right. Each wheel multiplies it by its own lock angle, then bends the result through a per-wheel Ackermann term so the two front wheels can end up at different angles, with that geometry expressed through the steering axis rather than hard-coded per side. Toe and camber are baked into the same wheel orientation, and caster tilts the steering axis so lock also feeds a little camber. An optional assist builds a clamp ceiling that starts at the driver command and blends toward the steering angle that produces peak lateral grip, blending in with squared speed and reaching full effect at roughly ten metres per second, then clips the command into that ceiling. The effect is that a keyboard or pad player gets usable lock at parking speed and a self-limiting steer angle once the car is loaded up.

constants.name: assistBlendPerSquaredSpeed
constants.unit: per square metre per second squared, saturating at 10 m/s, evaluated once per 1/90 s tick

constants.name: degreesPerPiRadians
constants.unit: degrees per pi radians, the conversion applied to setup toe, camber and caster once at load

cards.name: Coilover spring, damper and travel
cards.summary: Per-wheel spring rate, split compression and rebound damping, a travel limit and the rest-position offset implied by static wheel load
cards.behavior: Each corner carries a spring rate, a compression damping value, a rebound damping value, an anti-roll rate and a travel figure, all loaded from the car setup and all given defaults so a partially specified car still drives. The published travel is measured from the laden rest position, so at load time the model subtracts the static sag, computed as wheel load divided by spring rate, from zero and treats the rest as an offset inside the full mechanical range. That full range is what the wheel actually sweeps. Compression and rebound are separate setup numbers, though only the compression value is currently read back as the constraint damping, so rebound is a documented setup value without a consumer in this revision. The spring rate doubles as the stiffness fed to the suspension constraint row, so a soft car visibly rolls and pitches while a stiff one skips over bumps.

constants.name: springRateDefault
constants.unit: newtons per metre, applied every 1/900 s driveline substep

constants.name: compressionDampingDefault
constants.unit: newtons per metre per second of compression, applied every 1/900 s substep

constants.name: reboundDampingDefault
constants.unit: newtons per metre per second of extension, loaded at car setup and not consumed by the current constraint path

constants.name: travelFromRestDefault
constants.unit: metres of compression travel from the laden rest position, a static setup value, no per-tick rate

constants.name: unsprungInverseMassDefault
constants.unit: inverse kilograms, a 20 kg wheel and hub, used each 1/900 s substep

cards.name: Sampled suspension kinematics
cards.summary: Hinge geometry is evaluated at five travel stations and interpolated at runtime, so camber and track change come from the linkage
cards.behavior: Instead of integrating a linkage every tick, the loader solves the suspension geometry analytically for a double-wishbone layout, a MacPherson strut or a simple trailing hinge, then records wheel position and orientation at five evenly spaced travel stations between full droop and full bump. At runtime the current displacement is scaled into that four-interval table and both position and orientation are mixed linearly between the two nearest stations. A wishbone corner is solved as a circle-circle intersection in the upper hinge plane, a strut corner as a rotation about the lower hinge with the upright axis realigned, and the simple corner as a rotation about a single hinge. The practical effect is a wheel that gains negative camber and shifts inboard as it compresses, without paying for a constraint chain.

constants.name: travelStations
constants.unit: sampled travel stations per wheel, solved once at car load

constants.name: interpolationSegments
constants.unit: interpolation intervals between the five stations, read once per 1/90 s tick

cards.name: Slip ratio, slip angle and drive force
cards.summary: Slip is derived from wheel and contact velocities, then a magic-formula curve turns it into longitudinal and lateral force scaled by surface grip
cards.behavior: For each wheel the model compares the contact patch velocity with the wheel rotation speed. Longitudinal slip is the difference between rotational and forward speed over forward speed, with the divisor floored so a stationary car does not divide by zero; slip angle is the negative arctangent of lateral over forward speed. Load is converted to kilonewtons and capped so extreme suspension impulses cannot drive the curve into nonsense. Slip ratio is then rescaled by a hundred to express it in percent, which is the input convention the fitted coefficients expect, and the vertical load, camber and slip angle feed a magic-formula curve: a shape factor, a load-dependent peak, a low-slip stiffness that decays exponentially with load, a curvature factor and horizontal and vertical shifts. The resulting force is finally multiplied by the surface friction coefficient, so the same car keeps its full grip figure on asphalt and a smaller one on gravel.

constants.name: slipPercentScale
constants.unit: percent, converting slip ratio to the percent slip the curve is fitted in, each 1/900 s substep

constants.name: loadCeiling
constants.unit: kilonewtons of vertical load before the curve is clamped, each 1/900 s substep

constants.name: radiansToDegrees
constants.unit: degrees per pi radians, applied to slip angle and camber each 1/900 s substep

cards.name: Peak-slip lookup table
cards.summary: Peak-force slip values are solved numerically at build time into a table indexed by wheel load, and used to normalise driver aids
cards.behavior: The slip value that produces peak force depends on load, so the model does not use a single tuned constant. Instead the curve coefficients are assembled for one load, the peak is found by a Newton-Raphson search that walks the curve until the curvature-adjusted tangent reaches a quarter turn, stopping when the correction becomes tiny or after a small fixed number of steps. The resulting slip ratio and slip angle are stored in a table with a five-hundred-newton load step and twenty entries. The ratio is scaled by a hundredth so the percent-domain peak becomes a ratio again, and the angle is converted from degrees to radians. Because the table is filled once, the aids that need "the slip a fast driver would use" can read it in constant time every substep, and a heavy rear-engined car automatically wants a different slip angle from a light front-driver.

constants.name: tableLoadStep
constants.unit: newtons per table row, built once at car load

constants.name: tableEntries
constants.unit: load rows, covering 500 N to 10 kN, read each 1/900 s substep

constants.name: peakSlipRatioScale
constants.unit: ratio per percent slip, applied when the table is filled at car load

constants.name: peakSearchIterations
constants.unit: Newton-Raphson steps per load row, run once at car load

cards.name: Camber thrust and small-angle approximation
cards.summary: Camber is clamped, converted with a truncated series instead of an arcsine, and fed into both a lateral force shift and an extra slip velocity
cards.behavior: Camber enters the tyre in two ways. Inside the force curve it produces a horizontal shift, so a cambered tyre at zero slip angle still generates side force, and a vertical shift that biases the whole curve. Outside the curve, the model needs a slip velocity to represent the sideways drag a tilted wheel creates. Rather than calling an inverse sine it clamps the sine first and recovers the angle with a truncated cubic series, then uses a second truncated series for the tangent when it turns that angle into a velocity, so a car pitched onto two wheels cannot produce a wild value. The resulting slip velocity is added to the lateral row of the wheel constraint, which is what makes a leaning car wander and a well-cambered front end bite on turn-in.

constants.name: camberSineClamp
constants.unit: sine of camber angle, the clamp applied each 1/900 s substep

constants.name: arcsineSeriesDivisor
constants.unit: divisor of the cubic term in the arcsine series, each 1/900 s substep

constants.name: tangentSeriesDivisor
constants.unit: divisor of the cubic term in the tangent series, each 1/900 s substep

cards.name: Engine torque, friction and rev limiting
cards.summary: A tabulated torque curve scaled by throttle, minus a quadratic friction torque, with idle throttle solved at load and a hard rev limiter
cards.behavior: The engine is a shaft driven by two opposing torques. Combustion torque comes from a tabulated curve of flywheel torque against engine speed, scaled linearly by throttle, with the curve extended down to the stall speed and up to the rev limit by linear extrapolation from the outermost fitted points. Friction torque grows with engine speed as a quadratic, its three coefficients derived from displacement unless the car supplies its own, and is scaled by how far the throttle is closed. At load time the model also searches for the smallest throttle that keeps the engine turning at its start speed and derives a slope so idle throttle rises as speed drops and the engine will not stall at rest. Above the rev limit combustion is cut and the limit is dropped by a hundred revolutions so the engine does not chatter on the limiter, and a stalled engine gets ten times its friction.

constants.name: defaultRedline
constants.unit: revolutions per minute, a static setup value read every 1/90 s tick

constants.name: defaultRevLimit
constants.unit: revolutions per minute before combustion is cut, checked every 1/90 s tick

constants.name: defaultStallSpeed
constants.unit: revolutions per minute below which the engine is treated as stalled, checked every 1/90 s tick

constants.name: frictionLinearCoefficient
constants.unit: friction torque coefficient for the linear speed term, scaled by displacement at load and read every 1/90 s tick

constants.name: revLimitHysteresis
constants.unit: revolutions per minute of drop while the limiter is active, each 1/90 s tick

constants.name: stalledFrictionMultiplier
constants.unit: multiplier on friction torque while stalled, applied every 1/90 s tick

cards.name: Clutch capacity and automatic shifting
cards.summary: Clutch torque capacity comes from pressure, area and mean radius; an optional automatic clutch and shifter rate-limit engagement and pick gears from wheel speed
cards.behavior: Clutch capacity is computed once from plate pressure times friction area times the friction coefficient times the mean effective radius, and the transmitted torque is that capacity multiplied by pedal position, so a partially released clutch slips and a fully released one locks the engine to the gearbox. With the automatic clutch enabled, engagement is a control problem: above the start speed the clutch closes, and below it the closing is limited by how far the engine is above a floor that sits midway between stall and start speed, with the throttle leaning that floor. Engagement and disengagement are rate-limited asymmetrically, and mid-shift the clutch is opened and the throttle is either held or halved to smooth the torque cut. The automatic shifter watches clutch-side speed, selects the next gear when it passes the redline and drops a gear when it falls below a fraction of the redline scaled by the ratio gap.

constants.name: clutchFrictionCoefficient
constants.unit: unitless plate friction used in the capacity product, a static setup value, no per-tick rate

constants.name: clutchPlatePressure
constants.unit: pascals of clamping pressure, a static setup value, no per-tick rate

constants.name: clutchMeanRadius
constants.unit: metres, the mean effective friction radius, a static setup value, no per-tick rate

constants.name: clutchFrictionArea
constants.unit: square metres of friction surface, a static setup value, no per-tick rate

constants.name: defaultShiftTime
constants.unit: seconds, counted down once per 1/90 s tick while a shift is in progress

constants.name: autoClutchEngageRate
constants.unit: fraction of full clutch travel per second, so full engagement takes about 0.1 s at 1/90 s ticks

constants.name: downshiftSpeedFraction
constants.unit: fraction of redline in the lower gear before an automatic downshift, checked every 1/90 s tick

constants.name: shiftThrottleCut
constants.unit: fraction of throttle retained during a shift, applied every 1/90 s tick

cards.name: Limited-slip differential and drive layout
cards.summary: Final drive plus a speed-sensitive anti-slip coupling and an adjustable centre split decide how torque reaches the wheels
cards.behavior: Each differential carries a final drive ratio, an anti-slip torque, an optional torque-sensing term with a one-way or two-way factor, and a split value used by centre differentials. The driveline is assembled as a small network of shafts: the engine shaft, one shaft per driven wheel, and a coupling per differential whose softness is derived from the anti-slip torque and the substep so that the coupling reaches its maximum torque at a defined slip speed. Because the anti-slip behaviour is expressed as a coupling softness, a load coefficient and a per-substep impulse limit, a welded spool, a clutch-type limited slip and a viscous unit are all described by different numbers on the same coupling. Front-wheel, rear-wheel and all-wheel layouts select which differential feeds which shafts, and the all-wheel path multiplies a centre ratio into the total, so gearing feels different on each layout.

constants.name: defaultFinalDrive
constants.unit: unitless wheel revs per driveshaft rev, a static setup value, no per-tick rate

constants.name: defaultAntiSlipTorque
constants.unit: newton metres of locking torque before slip, applied every 1/900 s substep

constants.name: defaultTorqueSplit
constants.unit: unitless share of centre torque to the first side, a static setup value, no per-tick rate

constants.name: antiSlipReferenceSlipSpeed
constants.unit: radians per second of coupling slip at which anti-slip torque peaks, each 1/900 s substep

cards.name: Brake torque and ABS modulation
cards.summary: Brake torque scales with pedal, bias and handbrake; ABS limits how fast brake pressure may rise relative to predicted slip
cards.behavior: Brake capacity per wheel is pressure times pad area times pad friction times rotor radius, and applied torque is that capacity scaled by pedal travel times the bias plus the handbrake input times its own bias, with the handbrake deliberately kept on a separate factor so that the anti-lock loop cannot clamp it. With anti-lock enabled and the car moving above roughly four metres per second, the model extrapolates next tick slip from the change in slip over the last tick, compares it with the peak-slip table, and allows brake pressure to rise only by the remaining headroom, so pressure is released before the wheel actually locks. Below that speed, or with the aid off, the pedal value passes straight through. The result is a brake pedal that can be buried without spinning the car, and a handbrake that still locks the rear axle on demand.

constants.name: brakePadFriction
constants.unit: unitless pad-on-rotor friction, a static setup value, no per-tick rate

constants.name: brakeRotorRadius
constants.unit: metres of effective rotor radius, a static setup value, no per-tick rate

constants.name: brakePadArea
constants.unit: square metres of pad area, a static setup value, no per-tick rate

constants.name: absMinimumSquaredSpeed
constants.unit: square metres per second squared, so anti-lock engages above 4 m/s, checked every 1/90 s tick

constants.name: absPressureRiseGain
constants.unit: multiplier on the remaining slip headroom per tick, evaluated every 1/90 s tick

cards.name: Traction control
cards.summary: A throttle-side aid with hysteresis: it cuts throttle once slip passes the peak value by a margin and restores it only after slip falls well below
cards.behavior: Traction control works on the same peak-slip reference as the anti-lock loop but acts on the throttle rather than the brakes. It stays inactive until the driver asks for more than a tenth of throttle, then computes a target slip from the peak value tapered by the cosine of the current slip angle so it tightens up as the car slides sideways. The aid engages when measured slip exceeds the target by twenty percent and disengages only when slip falls below eighty percent of it, which prevents the on-off chatter a single threshold would produce. While engaged, commanded throttle is reduced in proportion to the excess slip scaled by clutch position and then clamped, so the car keeps the driver command as an upper bound instead of a fixed value. The feel is a rear end that steps out briefly and then hooks up.

constants.name: throttleActivationThreshold
constants.unit: fraction of full throttle, checked every 1/90 s tick

constants.name: slipEngageFactor
constants.unit: multiple of the peak slip value at which traction control cuts, each 1/90 s tick

constants.name: slipDisengageFactor
constants.unit: multiple of the peak slip value at which control releases, each 1/90 s tick

constants.name: throttleCorrectionGain
constants.unit: multiplier on excess slip per tick, applied every 1/90 s tick

cards.name: Surface friction, drag and road bumps
cards.summary: Each track surface carries separate tread and sidewall friction, a rolling resistance coefficient, a rolling drag and a sinusoidal bump field
cards.behavior: Surfaces are named types, each carrying a friction figure for the treaded part of the tyre and a separate one for the sidewall, so a car that slides on its shoulders loses less grip than one that slides flat. The per-wheel friction actually used is a linear blend between those two by the tyre tread fraction. Alongside friction each surface supplies a rolling resistance coefficient that scales a speed-proportional and a speed-squared resistance term, a rolling drag used as a velocity-proportional impulse that is clipped so it can never reverse a car, and a bump field described by a wavelength and an amplitude. Bump height is sampled as a smoothed triangular wave of the contact position in two horizontal axes, multiplied by amplitude and halved, then added to the suspension displacement. Switching from asphalt to grass therefore changes grip, drag and ride quality at once.

constants.name: surfaceAsphalt
constants.unit: surface type name matched once when track geometry is loaded, no per-tick rate

constants.name: defaultBumpWavelength
constants.unit: metres per bump cycle, sampled every 1/90 s tick

constants.name: bumpAmplitudeShare
constants.unit: fraction of surface bump amplitude added to travel, once per 1/90 s tick

cards.name: Ray against track patches
cards.summary: A ray is intersected with the nearest bounding-volume candidate patch by recursive parameter-quad subdivision, returning the hit patch for sector and surface lookup
cards.behavior: Track roads are stored as chains of four-by-four control-point surface patches, each linked to its successor and gathered into a bounding-volume index. A query first tests the patch the car was on last tick as a fast path, then asks the index for candidates near the ray. Each candidate is tested by repeatedly intersecting the ray with the flat quad spanned by the current parameter window and, on a hit, shrinking the window around the hit and testing again, so a curved patch is resolved to a small parameter region without tessellation. The hit with the smallest distance wins and the owning patch pointer travels back with the hit, which is what lets the game name a sector, look up a surface and tell the AI which piece of road it is on. Strip closure is detected by comparing endpoint corners within a small distance.

constants.name: subdivisionDepth
constants.unit: parameter-quad subdivision levels per patch, per ray, once per 1/90 s tick

constants.name: subdivisionAreaCut
constants.unit: fraction of the parameter window retained around a hit each level, per subdivision

constants.name: stripClosureTolerance
constants.unit: square metres of squared corner distance for a strip to count as closed, checked at load

cards.name: Corner speed limit and braking lookahead
cards.summary: Corner speed comes from patch curvature and a lateral friction factor; a braking-distance walk along the strip decides when to lift
cards.behavior: An opponent first reads the patch under its front wheels and trims it toward the racing line. It then asks for the speed that curvature and friction allow: the corner radius, widened by the road width when the next patch opens out, is fed into a maximum-speed solve that also accounts for aerodynamic lift changing the normal load, scaled by a lateral friction factor below the tyre peak so the driver has margin. The result is multiplied by a per-driver difficulty value. Locally, the difference between that limit and the car heading speed becomes throttle or brake through a proportional band with a dead zone, and both inputs are then rate-limited so the driver cannot stamp on the pedals. For corners further ahead, the driver walks forward along the strip for a distance equal to its own braking distance plus a margin and brakes fully as soon as a slower corner is closer than the distance needed to slow for it.

constants.name: speedBand
constants.unit: metres per second of speed error mapped to full throttle, evaluated every 1/90 s tick

constants.name: speedDeadBand
constants.unit: metres per second of overspeed tolerated before braking, evaluated every 1/90 s tick

constants.name: longitudinalFrictionFactor
constants.unit: fraction of tyre peak used for AI braking distance, evaluated every 1/90 s tick

constants.name: lateralFrictionFactor
constants.unit: fraction of tyre peak used for AI corner speed, evaluated every 1/90 s tick

constants.name: pedalRateLimit
constants.unit: fraction of full pedal travel per second, applied every 1/90 s tick

constants.name: brakingLookaheadMargin
constants.unit: metres added to the braking distance searched ahead, evaluated every 1/90 s tick

cards.name: AI steering lookahead and traffic analysis
cards.summary: Steering aims at a lookahead point accumulated patch by patch, while every other car is tracked in the driver frame for braking and overtaking
cards.behavior: Steering is pursuit along the road strip. The driver starts at the next patch and keeps advancing while the accumulated centreline distance is under one metre, adding twice each patch length per step, so it ends up aiming several car lengths ahead; the walk also stops early if the upcoming patch curves tighter than a minimum radius, which keeps the driver from cutting a hairpin. The destination is the centre of the front edge of the final patch. The angle between the car heading and the direction to that point, both flattened to the horizontal plane, is divided by the car maximum steering lock and clamped, and that becomes the steering command. Alongside steering, every tick projects every other car into the driver frame and records its fore distance, lateral offset, closing speed and an estimated time to contact, which is the data a driver would need to brake for a slow car or steer around one. The two bias helpers that consume that data express sensible intent: one builds a braking bias that multiplies ramps over reaction time, separation and closing speed, the other builds a lateral bias that saturates at a fixed spacing, but in this revision the hooks that would add those biases to the pedals and the steering angle are commented out, so only the analysis runs each tick.

constants.name: lookaheadPatchStride
constants.unit: patch-length multiplier per lookahead step, recomputed every 1/90 s tick

constants.name: lookaheadStartDistance
constants.unit: metres of centreline distance before the lookahead point is accepted, each 1/90 s tick

constants.name: sharpCornerRadius
constants.unit: metres of patch radius that aborts the lookahead walk, checked every 1/90 s tick

constants.name: steeringCommandClamp
constants.unit: fraction of maximum steering lock, clamped every 1/90 s tick

constants.name: trafficLateralCare
constants.unit: metres either side of the driver that count as in the way, evaluated every 1/90 s tick

constants.name: trafficBrakeStartDistance
constants.unit: metres of separation at which a braking bias would start, evaluated every 1/90 s tick

constants.name: avoidanceSpacing
constants.unit: metres of lateral offset targeted when steering around another car, each 1/90 s tick

cards.name: Generated racing line
cards.summary: A coarse-to-fine relaxation pass slides a lateral lane value at every road patch until curvature is minimised, respecting edge margins
cards.behavior: Each road patch in a strip becomes one node, with its left and right edge points taken from the patch corners and its lane value seeded at the middle of the road. The optimiser then works from coarse to fine: it starts with a large step and halves it down to one, and at each resolution it runs relaxation passes proportional to the square root of the step, moving every step-th node, then interpolates the nodes in between by matching a target curvature. A relaxation measures the inverse radius of the circle through the node and its two neighbours, nudges the lane value by a small Newton-like step toward a slightly larger radius, and then clamps the result against margins measured in from each edge and against the road width. Because the target curvature at each node is a length-weighted blend of the curvature measured at its two neighbours, the path converges to a smooth line that straightens corner entries rather than hugging the inside. The finished path and its per-node curvature are written back onto the strip for the drivers and the drawn racing line.

constants.name: securityRadius
constants.unit: metres of reference radius that scales the safety slack added to the edge margins, applied once per relaxation

constants.name: outsideMargin
constants.unit: metres of margin kept from the outer edge, applied once per relaxation

constants.name: insideMargin
constants.unit: metres of margin kept from the inner edge, applied once per relaxation

constants.name: relaxationsPerSqrtStep
constants.unit: relaxation passes per resolution level, multiplied by the square root of the step size, run once at track load

constants.name: initialSmoothingStep
constants.unit: patches in the first, coarsest smoothing step, halved each level at track load

constants.name: initialLaneValue
constants.unit: fraction from the left edge at seeding, written once per patch at track load

cards.name: Lap and sector timing
cards.summary: A lap counts when a wheel touches the next sector patch and the sector index wraps to zero; staging time is excluded from the clock
cards.behavior: Each car owns a running lap clock, a last and best lap, a sector index and an accumulated lap distance. Every tick the game computes the expected next sector as the current sector plus one modulo the sector count, then checks all four wheel contacts against that sector patch; a match advances the car to that sector. The car only records a completed lap when the advanced sector wraps back to zero, which is what stops a car parked on the finish patch from banking laps, and sector times are also written back as per-car-type records. The clock subtracts staging time while the countdown is running so the formation period is not charged to the lap. Lap distance is tracked separately for placement, which orders cars by completed laps and then by distance.

constants.name: stagingCountdown
constants.unit: seconds of counted-down staging removed from lap clocks, ticked down each 1/90 s tick

constants.name: sectorWrapIndex
constants.unit: sector index that closes a lap, compared every 1/90 s tick

constants.name: wheelsProbedPerLapCheck
constants.unit: wheel contacts tested against the sector patch, once per 1/90 s tick

cards.name: Drift scoring
cards.summary: Drift is the angle between heading and velocity above a speed floor, scored by distance travelled with speed and angle bonuses
cards.behavior: The scorer first requires the car to be on the track, meaning more than one wheel has a track patch, and moving faster than ten metres per second. It then flattens both heading and velocity to the horizontal plane and takes the angle between them. Drifting begins when that angle passes about eleven degrees and, once drifting, continues until it falls below about six degrees, which gives the state a wide hysteresis band so a wobble does not break a chain. Anything past a right angle is a spin and voids the drift. The base score is distance travelled while drifting, and the banked total adds a bonus of half the maximum speed reached plus about twelve times the maximum angle in radians, but only if the accumulated drift is worth more than a token amount, so a brief twitch scores nothing.

constants.name: driftSpeedFloor
constants.unit: metres per second, checked every 1/90 s tick

constants.name: driftEnterAngle
constants.unit: radians between heading and velocity, evaluated every 1/90 s tick

constants.name: driftExitAngle
constants.unit: radians, the relaxed threshold used once drifting, evaluated every 1/90 s tick

constants.name: bonusSpeedWeight
constants.unit: score per metre per second of peak drift speed, awarded once per banked drift

constants.name: bonusAngleWeight
constants.unit: score numerator per pi radians of peak drift angle, awarded once per banked drift

constants.name: bankThreshold
constants.unit: score points a drift must reach to be banked, checked once per 1/90 s tick

cards.name: Chase and orbit cameras
cards.summary: A chase rig carries an offset in car space and blends toward it; an orbit rig adds clamped yaw, pitch and distance
cards.behavior: The chase camera keeps a fixed offset in the car frame, two metres up and six metres behind, rotates that offset by the car orientation every frame and then moves toward the resulting target position with a blend proportional to frame time, capped so a long frame cannot snap it. Orientation is a look-at from the new position to the car, so the car is always centred and the camera lags into corners rather than rigidly following. The offset is validated so it can never sit in front of the car. The orbit camera is the photo rig: it holds a distance derived from the offset length, accumulates yaw and pitch from mouse or pad input with pitch clamped to about a radian and a half, and lets the user zoom the distance between one and four times the resting standoff. Both rigs orbit the same focus point, but only the chase rig derives its orientation by looking at the car; the orbit rig instead rebuilds its rotation from the accumulated yaw and pitch and places itself at the clamped distance along the rotated view axis.

constants.name: chaseHeight
constants.unit: metres above the car in car-local space, applied every frame

constants.name: chaseTrail
constants.unit: metres behind the car in car-local space, applied every frame

constants.name: positionBlendRate
constants.unit: per second of frame time, saturating to a snap, applied every rendered frame

constants.name: orbitRestingStandoff
constants.unit: multiples of the offset length along the forward axis, set when the orbit rig resets, no per-tick rate

constants.name: orbitPitchClamp
constants.unit: radians of accumulated pitch either way, applied every frame the rig rotates

cards.name: Analogue input shaping
cards.summary: Dead zone, gain, exponent and a signed button-to-axis ramp sit between the device and the car
cards.behavior: Raw device values are shaped before the car ever sees them. An axis first has its sign flipped if the binding is inverted, then a dead zone is removed by subtracting the threshold and rescaling the remainder back to full travel, then gain is applied and clipped to unit magnitude, and finally a response exponent is applied to the magnitude with the original sign restored, which lets a pad produce fine inputs near centre and still reach full lock. Buttons converted to axes use a ramp instead: the value moves toward the target at a configured rate rather than jumping, and the rate is deliberately asymmetric, climbing at roughly a quarter of the speed it falls, so releasing a key gives a faster return to neutral than pressing it. This is what makes keyboard driving in a physics-driven car usable at all.

constants.name: rampRiseScale
constants.unit: fraction of the configured ramp rate applied while pressing, per second of input time at 90 Hz

constants.name: rampFallScale
constants.unit: fraction of the configured ramp rate applied while releasing (signed so the value falls), per second of input time at 90 Hz

constants.name: gainClamp
constants.unit: magnitude ceiling after gain, applied every shaped axis read at 90 Hz

cards.name: Aerodynamic downforce and drag
cards.summary: Wings and bodywork add speed-squared lift and drag, with induced drag from the wing and reduced lift when travelling backwards
cards.behavior: Each aerodynamic device converts its setup numbers into coefficients once: a lift coefficient from half air density times the wing coefficient times wing area, an induced drag coefficient from that lift and the wing efficiency, and a drag coefficient from half density times the body coefficient times frontal area. Per tick, drag is the coefficient times wind speed times the wind vector, and lift is the coefficient times the square of the forward wind speed, pushed along the body up axis with the induced drag component pushed backwards. Wind speed is taken as the negative forward component, and if the car is travelling backwards the lift is scaled down sharply, so reversing produces little downforce. The downforce is applied at the wing position rather than the centre of mass, so a strong wing also changes the pitch balance, and it raises the load the tyres see, which is why top speed and corner speed trade directly.

constants.name: airDensity
constants.unit: kilograms per cubic metre, a static value folded into the coefficients at load

constants.name: dynamicPressureFactor
constants.unit: half, the dynamic-pressure factor applied once when coefficients are built at load

constants.name: reverseLiftFactor
constants.unit: fraction of lift retained when travelling backwards, applied every 1/90 s tick

cards.name: Suspension bump and landing events
cards.summary: A four-state machine turns suspension velocity and displacement into discrete bottoming hints for sound and effects
cards.behavior: Physics produces continuous travel, but sound and effects want discrete events. A small state machine watches suspension velocity and displacement: when velocity climbs past a threshold the state moves to displacing and starts a timer; if velocity stays high for the full timer window the state moves to displaced, and when velocity falls back the state moves to settling and holds until a second timer expires, then settles. Each transition is exposed as an edge the presentation layer can react to, along with start and end displacement, whose difference is the total size of the hit. Because both the velocity threshold and the timer lengths are explicit, a slow compression over a kerb and a hard landing off a raised patch look different to the audio and particle systems even though both end at full travel.

constants.name: displaceHoldTime
constants.unit: seconds of sustained compression before a bump is reported, ticked down every 1/90 s tick

constants.name: displaceVelocityThreshold
constants.unit: suspension travel per second, checked every 1/90 s tick

constants.name: settleHoldTime
constants.unit: seconds of settled travel before the event closes, ticked down every 1/90 s tick

cards.name: Skid marks and tyre squeal
cards.summary: Per-wheel squeal intensity from normalised slip feeds a decaying emitter that only lays a mark once enough energy accumulates
cards.behavior: Squeal is computed per wheel from the normalised slip ratio and slip angle: each is divided by its peak value from the load table, the two squares are summed, and the sum is multiplied by a clipped measure of contact patch velocity and then biased downward and clamped, so a wheel that is merely rolling reports nothing. The result drives a skid-mark emitter per wheel, which accumulates energy as a blend of the previous energy and the current intensity rather than following it directly. A mark is only laid, and only kept alive, once that energy exceeds a fixed threshold, so light cornering scrubs nothing while a locked wheel or a big slide immediately draws a ribbon. Body and wheel visuals are refreshed from the same physics read-back so the marks appear under the wheels that are actually sliding.

constants.name: emissionEnergyThreshold
constants.unit: accumulated squeal energy before a mark is laid, evaluated every 1/90 s tick

constants.name: emitterDecay
constants.unit: retained fraction of emitter energy per tick, blended every 1/90 s tick

constants.name: skidMarkBufferSlots
constants.unit: skid-mark segments retained in the ring buffer, restored when the system resets, no per-tick rate

constants.name: squealBias
constants.unit: offset subtracted from the squeal product before clamping, applied every 1/90 s tick

cards.name: Replay input deltas and keyframes
cards.summary: Replays store only changed inputs plus periodic car state snapshots, replayed by re-running the same dynamics
cards.behavior: A replay is not a recorded animation. While recording, each car writes an input frame only when at least one control value differs from the previous stored value, so long periods of steady throttle cost almost nothing, and every thirtieth frame it also writes a full state snapshot with the serialised car state and the input vector at that instant. During playback the recorded inputs are fed back into the same car dynamics at the same fixed step, and the periodic snapshots are used to seek or to resynchronise. Because the simulation is deterministic at a fixed tick and the input stream is exact, the replayed car follows the original line without any position stream at all, and seek is a matter of restoring the nearest snapshot and replaying forward.

constants.name: keyframeInterval
constants.unit: recorded frames between full state snapshots, at one recorded frame per 1/90 s tick
